_about: One authored sentence per species, keyed on the collection's own common_name. Kept to what is uncontroversial about the plant or its arrival in American orchards; the second half of every on-screen blurb is computed from the database at render time, so the numbers are never hand-maintained. Add a key here and it appears; leave one out and the composition simply omits the line.
apples: Brought west from the Tian Shan mountains of Central Asia, where its wild ancestor Malus sieversii still grows; every named variety is a graft, since a pip never breeds true to its parent.
peaches: Domesticated in China at least 4,000 years ago and carried along the Silk Road; Spanish colonists planted it so early that later settlers mistook it for a native tree.
pears: A European pear ripens properly only off the tree — picked hard and softened in storage, which is why so many of these plates show fruit that never looked ripe on the branch.
plums: The domestic plum is thought to be a natural hybrid of the sloe and the cherry plum; North America had its own wild plums, which orchardists here were crossing with the European kind.
grapes: Nearly every wine grape on earth is one species, Vitis vinifera — but it survives today on American rootstock, which is resistant to the phylloxera aphid that destroyed Europe's vineyards in the 1870s.
strawberries: The garden strawberry is an accident of empire: a chance cross in a French garden between a Virginian species and a Chilean one, neither of which makes a large berry alone.
oranges: Not a wild species but an ancient hybrid of pummelo and mandarin, reconstructed so long ago in southern China that no wild orange has ever been found.
cherries: Dwarfing rootstocks for sweet cherry only arrived late in the 20th century; the orchards these were painted for grew full-size trees, and were worked from ladders.
grapefruits: A Caribbean accident, first recorded in Barbados in the 1750s as a cross between pummelo and sweet orange; it takes its name from growing in grape-like clusters.
avocados: The tree flowers in two shifts — each blossom opens female, closes, and reopens male the next day — so growers interplant varieties on opposite rhythms to improve fruit set.
persimmons: Astringent until fully soft, because unripe flesh is loaded with tannins that bind to the proteins in saliva; the fruit is not sour, it is briefly leathery.
lemons: A hybrid of citron and sour orange, and the citrus that made long sea voyages survivable once the Royal Navy connected its juice to the prevention of scurvy.
mangoes: A relative of poison ivy and the cashew, which is why handling the peel raises a rash on some people while the flesh is perfectly harmless.
crab apple: Any apple under two inches across, by the old orchardists' rule. Too sharp to eat raw, but rich in pectin, which is what sets a jelly.
Japanese apricot: Grown across East Asia for its blossom as much as its fruit, which opens on bare wood in late winter and is almost never eaten fresh.
blackberries: Botanically not a berry but a cluster of tiny stone fruits, each with its own seed; the white core that stays behind on a raspberry comes away with a blackberry.
limes: The most cold-sensitive of the common citrus, which confined American groves to Florida and the far southern coast.
nectarines: A peach with a single recessive gene switched off — the one that grows the fuzz. A peach tree can throw a nectarine branch, and a nectarine stone can grow a peach.
pummelos: The largest citrus, and one of the three wild ancestors — with the mandarin and the citron — from which every other cultivated citrus was hybridised.
black raspberries: A North American native, distinct from the European red raspberry, and the parent of the purple hybrids that orchardists were breeding when these were painted.
bananas: Cultivated bananas are sterile triploids propagated entirely by cuttings, so a commercial variety is one enormous clone — and vulnerable to a single disease.
gooseberries: Banned from much of the United States for decades after 1911: Ribes carries white pine blister rust, and the timber industry won the argument.
loquats: Flowers in autumn and ripens in spring, backwards from every other tree in the orchard, which is why it fruits reliably only where winters are mild.
quinces: Too hard and sour to eat raw, but its flesh turns pink and perfumed with long cooking; the word marmalade comes from marmelo, the Portuguese for quince.
tangelos: A deliberate cross of tangerine and pummelo or grapefruit, made by USDA breeders themselves — several were named and released in the years these plates were painted.
cherry plum: One of the two wild parents of the domestic plum, grown in its own right for fruit that ripens weeks before anything else in the orchard.
figs: Not a fruit but an inflorescence turned outside in — hundreds of flowers lining a hollow stem, pollinated in some varieties by a wasp that enters and dies inside.
citron: The oldest citrus in Mediterranean cultivation, grown almost entirely for its thick peel rather than its scant flesh.
hickory: A North American genus of nut trees, and the one whose timber was valued enough that the nuts were often an afterthought.
pomegranates: Each seed is wrapped in its own juice-filled sac, an aril; the fruit is technically a berry with a leathery rind.
red raspberries: The receptacle stays on the plant when you pick one, leaving the berry hollow — the simplest way to tell it from a blackberry in the field.
sapodillas: Source of chicle, the latex that was the base of chewing gum before synthetics replaced it.
tangerines: A mandarin selection, and one of the few cultivated citrus close to a true wild species rather than a hybrid of them.
chayote: A squash relative from Mesoamerica with a single large seed, eaten as a vegetable but catalogued here with the fruit.
olives: Inedible straight from the tree — the bitterness is oleuropein, which has to be cured out in brine or lye before the fruit is food.
pecans: The tree nut of greatest commercial importance native to North America, and still largely gathered from wild river-bottom groves when these were painted.
American cranberry: Grown in bogs not because it needs water but because flooding makes harvest possible: ripe berries have air pockets and float.
blueberries: Effectively undomesticated until the 1910s, when Elizabeth White and Frederick Coville selected the first cultivated highbush varieties — work contemporary with these plates.
cherimoyas: Custard-textured and hand-pollinated in cultivation, because its natural pollinator does not live outside its native Andean range.
brambles: The catch-all genus Rubus, which hybridises so freely that botanists have named hundreds of microspecies and still argue about them.
citranges: A USDA hybrid of sweet orange and the hardy trifoliate orange, bred to push citrus north; the fruit is poor but the rootstock is excellent.
custard apple: An Annona of the tropical Americas, too soft-skinned to ship, which kept it a dooryard fruit rather than a commercial one.
pineapples: A bromeliad, not a tree fruit — and a fused cluster of dozens of individual berries around a single stem.
tangors: A tangerine-sweet orange cross, peeling like a mandarin but with the juice of an orange.
walnuts: The husk stains everything it touches with juglone, the same compound the roots release to suppress plants growing nearby.
apricots: Ripens earlier than any other stone fruit and blooms earliest too, which is exactly why late frosts ruin the crop so often.
raspberries: A cluster of tiny drupelets that separates cleanly from its core, leaving the thimble shape that gives the fruit its form.
currants: Banned alongside gooseberries as a host of white pine blister rust; the federal restriction was not lifted until 1966.
almonds: The stone of a fruit closely related to the peach — what is eaten is the kernel, and the leathery hull is the discarded flesh.
chestnuts: The American chestnut was a dominant eastern forest tree when these were painted, and was all but erased by blight within forty years.
guavas: Seeds pass through birds intact, which has made it one of the most invasive fruit trees in the tropics it was carried to.
papayas: Grows as a giant herb rather than a tree — the trunk is not wood — and yields papain, long used to tenderise meat.
mulberries: Grown across Eurasia less for fruit than for leaves, the sole food of the domesticated silkworm.
elderberries: Edible cooked and best avoided raw: the stems and unripe fruit carry cyanogenic compounds that heat drives off.
jujube: The Chinese date, dried rather than eaten fresh in most of its range, and one of the most drought-hardy fruit trees in cultivation.
kaki: The Japanese persimmon, selected over centuries into both astringent and non-astringent types — the latter edible while still crisp.
medlar: Eaten only after bletting, a controlled softening past ripeness that sounds like rot and is the point of the fruit.
feijoas: The petals are sweet and edible, and in its native South America birds eat them and pollinate the flower in the same visit.
carissa: A thorny South African shrub whose fruit is edible while every other part of the plant carries a milky latex that is not.
